title: Pair charged over RAF Fairford plot to face trial next November
description: Two British nationals charged in connection with an alleged plot linked to Iran at RAF Fairford last month will go on trial next year, a court has bee
body: Two British nationals charged in connection with an alleged plot linked to Iran at RAF Fairford last month will go on trial next year, a court has been told.London's Old Bailey heard from lawyers representing Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and 25-year-old Nouman Essghir that the pair would be denying wrongdoing, so a date for a four-week trial was set for Woolwich Crown Court from 22 November 2027. The two men, both from London, appeared via videolink charged under the National Security Act after vans packed with petrol were driven to the airbase in Gloucestershire in September. Julia Faure Walker, prosecuting, said both defendants were in contact with a person named Ali who was acting "in the interests" of Iran. A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.During the hearing on Friday, both defendants confirmed their identities and their lawyers indicated both would deny the charges against them.  Abdulkarim, from Westminster, is accused of assisting a foreign intelligence service. It is alleged he acted as an "intermediary" for Ali, who was not in the UK and allegedly directed the operation.Prosecutors allege he aided Ali, and bought equipment for the mission and received a number of payments from him totalling around £70,000.  Essghir, from Notting Hill,  is charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, in relation to an alleged "reconnaissance" mission on 22 August. He is accused of filming the perimeter of RAF Fairford at Ali's request. Essghir was among the five men arrested on 27 September, and was then re-arrested on 20 October. After the hearing, Essghir was remanded in custody while Abdulkarim was granted continued bail.  Iran has previously denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.The base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for it to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.After the incident in September the US pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base, without giving specific details.

schema.headline: Pair charged over RAF Fairford plot to face trial next November

title: Andy Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more
description: Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it
body: Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it had become, if nothing else, a confusing day.That confusion was unleashed by an EU official who briefed reporters in the morning that implementing the new arrangements on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions would be contingent on the government agreeing within six months to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying in Britain.That was later qualified by others in the EU - and straightforwardly disputed by the British government. And for all that it dominated the morning, it did not ultimately dominate or particularly overshadow what was a warm press conference between the prime minister and his EU counterparts, Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.The settled position appears to be that negotiations on student fees will continue into the next six months but on a separate track, or a "different sheet of paper" as von der Leyen put it. This still carries some degree of political risk for Burnham, because if Britain agrees to reduce, let alone equalise, university fees that would be an economic hit for universities which would presumably end up being covered by the government. And it may still be possible, though probably unlikely, that a deterioration in those negotiations could pollute the progress of today's agreements.Conversely, expect Burnham and his ministers to talk up another area where negotiations will continue - on the UK not being affected by the EU's "Made in Europe" plans, an attempt by the bloc to protect its industries from Chinese competition.Today's achievements and hiccups alike may quickly pale into insignificance anyway. At the dramatic conclusion of his first party conference speech as Labour leader in September - a moment he has been dreaming of for decades - the prime minister vowed to get closer to the EU.Over the subsequent two months it has at times been a bit unclear how exactly he envisages that playing out and quite how far he is willing to go. But focusing on the process risks obscuring the most important development, which is that the prime minister and the government are now unambiguously committed to Britain not only getting closer, but getting much closer to the EU.There were two significant moments at today's summit in that regard.First, Burnham said that the government had got as far as it could go with incremental deals with the EU, at least this side of a general election. In other words, he has got as far as he believes is possible with the strategy he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer of getting closer to the EU within the confines of the post-Brexit architecture set out by Theresa May all those years ago, of Britain remaining outside the single market and the customs union. That suggests that after two years of this, there will not be a third annual summit to unveil specific agreements designed to smooth post-Brexit issues affecting specific sectors.Yet it does sound like there will be another summit next year - or, rather, an "informal brainstorming process" about potential options for future relations with the EU. That sounds pretty nebulous, sure, but an event dedicated specifically to both sides discussing how to change the terms of Britain's arrangements with the EU is likely to become quite a big moment when it arrives. Perhaps as importantly, von der Leyen made clear that the EU was embracing this event too. That said, it does diminish the chances of major movement from Burnham towards embracing a specific model for the EU relationship in the intervening period.And what of the domestic politics of this? Britain's seventh prime minister in just over 10 years watched from Manchester as the fraught relationship with Europe wrecked the careers of so many of those predecessors.Burnham's gamble is that this time it's different. He believes that public regret about how Brexit has played out opens the political space for a far-reaching renegotiation. Plenty of Labour MPs enthusiastically agree, and see this as the route to uniting the "progressive" vote at the next election too. Some, especially those who represent Labour's former industrial heartlands, are a little more apprehensive.This morning's confusion is a reminder that there is another element to this gamble. Negotiating with Brussels, even if both sides believe progress is a "win-win", can be a fraught and complicated business. Once he's on the other side of his brainstorm, can Burnham carry that off without getting bogged down and distracting from his government's other priorities?On the day he became Labour leader in July, Burnham described it as the biggest change moment in British politics in 40 years. He was talking principally about economic transformation. But going to Brussels and getting what he wants without serious complications would be a pretty big change too.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

title: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster IPO
description: Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sel
body: Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sell off continues.The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.However, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 10% to about $87.30, close to its IPO price of $83, and the broader stock market declines seen on Thursday continued.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.8% in morning trade, the S&P 500 was down 1.2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely flat.The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth."As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said."Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

schema.headline: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster IPO

title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
description: A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.This is "not working the way it should b
body: A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses. A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection. Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour. Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain". He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen. "He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"

schema.headline: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour

title: Pat Cummins retains support of Cricket Australia as Test captain despite sandpaper allegations
description: Pat Cummins will retain backing from Cricket Australia (CA) to remain as Test captain despite ongoing and explosive allegations about the sandpaper co
body: Pat Cummins will retain backing from Cricket Australia (CA) to remain as Test captain despite ongoing and explosive allegations about the sandpaper controversy.A detailed testimony from Cameron Bancroft supported previous claims made by Usman Khawaja that the entire Australia team - including Cummins - knew of the plan to tamper with the ball during a Test match against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.Cummins has always denied involvement in or knowledge of the cheating plot, and reiterated his stance in a 68-minute address to the media last week.CA has regularly spoken of its support for Cummins, and the fast bowler will be allowed to continue in the captaincy role he has held since 2021. A statement could be issued over the weekend.Cummins, 33, is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December. A squad for the series opener against the Black Caps has not yet been named.With the support of CA, a decision on Cummins' future as captain would now appear to rest with the player, who has shown no indication he will resign.The row over the sandpaper saga, one of the biggest controversies in Test history, has engulfed Australian sport since Khawaja's claims first emerged two weeks ago.In 2018, Bancroft, then-captain Steve Smith and his vice-captain David Warner were punished for Bancroft's act of rubbing sandpaper on the ball in the third Test against South Africa at Newlands.Khawaja, who retired from international cricket earlier this year, wrote in his autobiography that the entire Australian team knew and should have taken responsibility.The former batter's account was supported by his childhood friend Warner, along with Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland, both back-up bowlers on the tour.In response, Cummins called a news conference where he promised to answer all questions about his part in the controversy, in the hope of "never having to speak about it again".He called Khawaja's assertions "100% wrong" and "nonsense".However, Cummins' address to the media motivated Bancroft to publish his own account of more than 4,000 words in the West Australian newspaper."The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft."It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone."Bancroft alleged he had conversations with all of the bowlers about how much the ball was swinging, and that the entire group of players and coaches celebrated when the ball-tampering yielded success.Batter Bancroft also implicated Darren Lehmann, who was then the Australia head coach, and David Saker, the bowling coach.Lehmann, now the coach of county side Northamptonshire, is due to commentate for the BBC and Australian radio station ABC on the first T20 between Australia and England in Melbourne on Saturday.Saker was part of the England coaching staff for the one-day tri-series in Pakistan in October.The 60-year-old has been employed by England on an ad hoc consultancy basis, an arrangement that has now ended.England have firmed up new coaching teams under Test head coach Stephen Fleming and his white-ball counterpart Brendon McCullum.

schema.headline: Pat Cummins retains support of Cricket Australia as Test captain despite sandpaper allegations

title: BepiColombo spacecraft arriving at Mercury after eight years
description: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage Figure caption, Why is a spacecraft flying to Mercury?ByRebec
body: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage Figure caption, Why is a spacecraft flying to Mercury?ByRebecca MorelleAlison Francis  and Tony Jolliffe BBC News Science After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface."I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission."There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."Image source, ESA/JAXAImage caption, The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018, launching from French Guiana.With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury -  to slow it down enough to get into orbit.This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity. If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.Image source, NASAImage caption, A close up view of the scarred surface of Mercury Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.Image source, NASAImage caption, These strange hollows have not been seen anywhere else in the Universe As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history."One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained."Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.Image source, Tony Jolliffe/BBC NewsImage caption, A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in LondonUnusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate. An ESA craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to JAXA, will view the planet from a distance.A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features  - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect."We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall."It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gently… As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.

schema.headline: BepiColombo spacecraft arriving at Mercury after eight years

title: GTA 6 drives spike in download demand, as estimated sales top $2.3bn
description: Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to be the biggest entertainment launch in history after the blockbuster video game debuted on Thursday, following a 13
body: Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to be the biggest entertainment launch in history after the blockbuster video game debuted on Thursday, following a 13-year wait.Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch. New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access.Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than 24.5 million units, making about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics site Sensor Tower.In comparison, this year's highest-grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas.GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both firms for comment.In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times in the US East Coast. In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany.The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

schema.headline: GTA 6 drives spike in download demand, as estimated sales top $2.3bn

title: Man Utd drone incident: Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola says filming training sessions by drone should be illegal
description: Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start
body: Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start Sunday's match."We've faced each other and obviously he [Pochettino] has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at," said Iraola."We can look at games from the US but it's true that they have this small advantage that we don't have references to prepare, because they can go different ways that we honestly don't know right now."Iraola said he expected United to be "well prepared" as Pochettino's assistants travelled to England to work with the players before the Argentine arrived on Wednesday."They have this advantage that we don't exactly know - or at least we don't have the references like we do against other opposition," he said."Especially the beginning of the game will be important. We have to adapt to certain things. But we know the players very well."Liverpool are fourth in the table - 14 places ahead of United.But they have failed to beat the Red Devils at Anfield in each of the past three seasons, and have lost to Arsenal and Manchester City at home already in this campaign."You don't find bigger games than this," said Iraola. "I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be a part of these games."We have to acknowledge the importance of the game. There are a lot of ingredients. They have a new manager, new challenges for us. This is important for us in a lot of different ways."We want to improve our form at home. We have been very good away but not good at home and the first chance we have is United on Sunday."

schema.headline: Man Utd drone incident: Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola says filming training sessions by drone should be illegal

title: Chelsea: How Joao Pedro is becoming Blues' most important player
description: Who is Chelsea's most important player?Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo are names that would probably feature in any debate, but Joao Pedro's recent abs
body: Who is Chelsea's most important player?Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo are names that would probably feature in any debate, but Joao Pedro's recent absence has certainly strengthened the argument in his favour.The debate started again among Blues fans over the past couple of weeks following their 1-0 defeat by Sunderland, the latest in a run of poor results without the Brazil striker.The 25-year-old will miss Leeds United's visit on Saturday with a thigh injury after Chelsea lost three of their previous four matches without him, although one defeat came in a penalty shootout against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.Having suffered a 2-0 home defeat by Tottenham in that run, manager Xabi Alonso has faced criticism over his side's lack of identity and some of his personnel decisions, particularly when attempting to replace Joao Pedro.Danny Welbeck, who was expected to provide cover after his summer arrival from Brighton, has started only one Premier League match during Joao Pedro's injury absence.Instead, Pedro Neto has twice been deployed through the middle, in the home win over Manchester United and the defeat by Sunderland, while Morgan Rogers started as the central striker against Spurs.Striker Emmanuel Emegha, signed from Strasbourg over the summer, hasn't started a league game but has struggled with fitness issues of his own. The continued absence of Joao Pedro is certainly proving costly before the busy winter schedule, with fifth-placed Chelsea already 11 points behind Premier League leaders Arsenal.Having been handed both a new contract until 2034 and the number nine shirt vacated by Liam Delap in August, Chelsea regard their £55m signing from Brighton in 2025 as a key figure in Alonso's plans.Asked about scoring more goals without the striker on Friday, Alonso said: "Yes, we need the whole team for that. It's not just the strikers who can score, we can score in set-pieces from defenders, midfielders, so it's teamwork for sure. "Joao is an important player but we need to be this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player. "The other players, they need to step up and they need to show that they are ready to compete and ready to play for Chelsea."There is little doubt Alonso has suffered when Joao Pedro has been unavailable, as did his predecessors. The numbers are undeniable.Since the start of the 2025-26 Premier League season, Chelsea have averaged 1.8 goals per game with Joao Pedro, compared to 0.6 without.Their expected goals (xG) drop from 1.8 per game with him to 1.1 without, highlighting a decline in Chelsea's attacking output rather than simply their finishing.Chelsea average 4.8 shots on target per game when the Brazilian plays, compared with 3.9 when he does not.Chelsea have failed to score in only 12.2% of Premier League matches involving him, compared with 71.4% when he has been absent.Those numbers are also reflected in the results.Chelsea have lost without scoring in just 7.3% of league games featuring Joao  Pedro, compared with 71.4% without him. Three of their Premier League defeats this season were without him, while they have scored in every game that he has featured. Chelsea's points-per-game average falls from 1.5 to 0.9 when he is unavailable.Joao Pedro, who has also operated as a number 10 and on the wing for Chelsea, appears to improve the output of those around him.During the past season and a half, Palmer has played 2,317 Premier League minutes alongside him and 528 without him.Palmer has scored 12 goals and registered four assists with the Brazil forward in the side, equating to 0.6 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Without him, Palmer has managed one goal and no assists, equivalent to 0.2 goal involvements per 90.Palmer's chance creation actually increases when Joao Pedro is absent, rising from 1.4 chances created per 90 minutes to 1.9. However, his goals return falls from 0.5 per 90 to 0.2, suggesting the striker's presence is more closely linked to Palmer's goalscoring output than his creativity.The pair have developed a productive partnership. Joao Pedro has assisted four Palmer goals, while Palmer has provided three assists to the ex-Brighton forward.. There is less data available for Rogers given his more recent arrival, but the trend is similar.Rogers has played 523 Premier League minutes alongside Joao Pedro and 360 without him. With Joao Pedro available, Rogers averages 0.7 goals per 90 minutes and 0.9 goal involvements per 90. Without him, those figures fall to 0.3 goal involvements per 90.While the sample size remains relatively small, the figures suggest Chelsea's attacking players generally produce more when Joao Pedro plays.All three of his assists this season have been for either Rogers or Palmer, sparking early season excitement about Chelsea's new trio, with nicknames like 'JP Morgan' and 'CPR' having been given to them. With 20 goals and eight assists, Joao Pedro has been directly involved in 36.4% of Chelsea's 77 Premier League goals since joining the club.Whether he is the Blues' most important player remains open to debate. The statistics do show, however, that their points return with him in the side is consistent with Champions League qualification, whereas their return without him is not. Alonso's team have yet to demonstrate they can perform at the same level when the Brazilian is unavailable.

schema.headline: Chelsea: How Joao Pedro is becoming Blues' most important player

title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
description: Image caption, Many of the companies marketing supported housing investments were linked to developer Lee JonesByNalini SivathasanBBC News Investigati
body: Image caption, Many of the companies marketing supported housing investments were linked to developer Lee JonesByNalini SivathasanBBC News Investigations and Mitchell Labiakbusiness reporter"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.Image caption, The BBC saw mould on ceilings and overflowing rubbish when we visited Castleview HouseProviders offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support.Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment. We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.Image caption, Promotional materials such as this social media post advertise the homes as "Secure, Government-Backed Wealth"'Total dishonesty' in marketingLee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat."Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."Image caption, Marketing images appeared to show Castleview House as newly refurbished with bright white interiorsPhil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan Hála had been coming through the letterbox for months.Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.Jan Hála, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the Britské Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.According to the Regulator of Social Housing, this would mean it was providing a high level of care, equivalent to living in a care home.But Nurture had not been registered as a specialised supported housing provider, the regulator said, and its claim to be providing this was "shocking".In a statement, Nurture acknowledged that Castleview House is managed under a "general housing management model" and does not form part of its supported housing portfolio. It said it provided supported housing elsewhere through partners which were registered providers.It said the Czech advert found by the BBC related to "historic marketing material" produced by third parties.However, the BBC has seen marketing material from several other agents selling flats in Castleview House to investors, which also claim that Nurture is providing supported housing to the residents on a 25-year lease.Nurture said it is not directly involved with the companies marketing the properties. But it said: "We will be reviewing communications with relevant agents and reminding them of the importance of ensuring that any information relating to Nurture is accurate, transparent and does not create misunderstanding regarding the accommodation or services provided."'No-one is directly accountable'While there are doubts about what kind of housing Nurture has been providing, the BBC also found other flats sold to investors overseas with tenants who were in supported exempt accommodation.The web of companies involved in providing this housing and cross-border ownership means it can be difficult for vulnerable tenants to get help when there are problems with properties."The way that the current system works is there's different levels of involvement by different organisations and companies and no-one is directly accountable," Abena Oppong-Asare, the housing committee chairwoman, told us.Mo, who has mental health issues, was housed in a studio flat in Cricklewood, north London, after he became homeless. The converted house containing his flat was bought by Gemelli London 2 Limited, a company run by French nationals living in the Czech Republic, for £1.83m in January last year.Image caption, Mo (right) pictured with a friend who also lived in the same building, says his ceiling collapsed and was not fixed for months He says his supported housing provider, Windrush Alliance, receives nearly £2,000 a month via Barnet Council for the flat. Mo says he receives £340 in universal credit for living expenses every month - but he is expected to pay Windrush a monthly £120 service charge out of that.Last year his ceiling collapsed after a leak went unrepaired for more than a year and Mo was temporarily housed in another flat in the property.Mo says his weekly visits from a Windrush support worker feel like a tick-box exercise and do not help him with the mental health issues which have been keeping him out of work.Gemelli's director Stephane Boussier told the BBC that when the company bought the property "no complaints from residents were disclosed". It was made aware of issues in August 2025, he said, and since then has "raised them with Windrush in writing, inspected the property and pressed for them to be resolved".He added that Gemelli London 2 Limited receives about £1,365 per flat per month from Windrush and does not receive any of the extra housing benefit that would be used for vulnerable tenants.Windrush said it was aware of issues at Mo's property and was "working with the building owner to put them right". According to Gemelli, the ceiling was repaired after the BBC contacted the two companies.Windrush has previously been criticised by the Regulator for Social Housing for a "failure to meet the standards" of the regulator, including failing to ensure "tenants are safe in their homes".It acknowledged that it "fell short in the past". It wrote off £1.8m in "funds to former directors and companies under their control", saying the company's financial position had been "compromised" by their actions. The company now has a new board in place.Windrush told us its "priority is residents, not investors" and the rates it charges "are agreed with the relevant local authorities" and "any surplus is reinvested in our homes and services".'The worst kind of exploitation'In Bradford, the BBC visited City Exchange and Colonnade House, two former office blocks which Lee Jones has converted into housing - with Nurture Housing Association managing many of the flats. Many of the properties there were advertised as supported housing investments. Residents showed us cockroach infestations, faulty fire alarms, broken lifts, leaks through the ceiling and black mould.Nurture Housing said it was only responsible for the individual homes that it manages and does not manage communal areas or "wider building infrastructure"."Nurture Housing and its managing agents regularly raise these concerns with the block manager," the company said.The freeholder for Phil's block, Castleview House, and City Exchange, blamed "defects" by the developer Lee Jones for the problems with the buildings and said it was taking legal action. Colonnade House has had several building management companies in recent years and the latest said it was addressing the problems.None of these companies or individuals are breaking the law, but critics say they are exploiting a lack of regulation in the sector.Three years after the Supported Housing Act was passed in England, which would put in place a licensing regime for supported housing providers and give local councils more powers to shut down providers that failed to meet the standards, it still has not been implemented."It's taken too long," said Jasmine Basran, head of policy and campaigns at housing charity Crisis. "In the meantime, this an area where we've seen the worst kind of exploitation."Additional reporting by Lorna Acquah and Abi SmittonGet in touchHave you been affected by issues covered in this story?   Share your experiences.

schema.headline: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad

title: Ireland v South Africa: Defiant Boks set to front up without banned Rassie Erasmus
description: 'No-one is going to break us' - defiant Boks face Ireland without ErasmusImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Siya Kolisi (right) spoke passionate
body: 'No-one is going to break us' - defiant Boks face Ireland without ErasmusImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Siya Kolisi (right) spoke passionately about what rugby means to South African people in his pre-match news conferenceByMatt GaultBBC Sport NI senior journalistAlready circled as one of the must-see fixtures in a packed November schedule, interest in the meeting between Ireland and South Africa has intensified following their contrasting disciplinary fortunes in recent days.Not for the first time, Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus landed himself in hot water with the powers-that-be for criticising match officials. After receiving a six-match ban for questioning the integrity of referee Andrea Piardi and television match official Matteo Liperini in South Africa's defeat by France last week, Erasmus has attracted praise and condemnation. Any doubt about where his players stand, however, was cleared up by captain Siya Kolisi, who bristled at a suggestion Erasmus was being "dramatic". "It might sound dramatic to you, but to us it means so much more," Kolisi said during his pre-match news conference. "Rugby has done a lot for our country, and it's done a lot for many of us who come from South Africa."We know how happy people are and what the mood is like when we win, and when we lose, it gets tough. People care a lot about it."When we play, we think about the people back home. We don't take representing the country lightly because we represent every single person in South Africa when we put on that jersey."Ireland v South AfricaNations ChampionshipSaturday 21 November, 16:40 GMTAviva Stadium, DublinLive on 5 Sports Extra, BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentaryWhile Erasmus has dominated headlines this week, he will not be in attendance at Aviva Stadium on Saturday.Instead, in a bizarre twist, the two-time World Cup winner will host a watchalong of the game from the team's Dublin hotel, with the conditions of his suspension prohibiting him from matchday contact with players and management."He's been hands-on with our team [in the build-up], and we're in a good space," assistant coach Mzwandile Stick said of Erasmus. "Irrespective of what has happened, we love him, we appreciate him, and no-one is going to break us. I can tell you that for sure."Whether or not Jasper Wiese joins Erasmus' stream remains to be seen. The back row was hit with a four-match ban for a dangerous ruck clearout against France. While Wiese's fate did not attract the same level of scrutiny, South Africa's sense of injustice will perhaps be fuelled by the sight of Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast on Saturday. As predicted by Erasmus, Prendergast was cleared to face the world champions after successfully appealing against his citing for an alleged hip-drop tackle on Fiji back row Peceli Yato. "I will tell you now for free, if that was a Fijian player tackling an Irish player with that hip-drop, that player would be in Fiji now," said Stick."If that was a Fijian player, he would be sitting in Fiji now doing some extra lessons of how to tackle."Ireland focused on erasing scrum painImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dan Sheehan says he is not fazed by switching to the back of the scrumFocused on erasing the pain of last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, Ireland have sidestepped questions about Erasmus this week, with head coach Andy Farrell opting not to comment on his opposite number's suspension."Obviously it's a big media story for fans to get behind," said captain Dan Sheehan. "But in terms of us playing the match it has zero impact."While there may be added scrutiny on referee Christophe Ridley, Sheehan said he plans to leave the official alone unless compelled to bring something "major" to his attention. The Irish skipper has enough on his plate anyway. In addition to leading his side against the back-to-back world champions, Sheehan has been thrust into the number eight role. The 28-year-old has won all 42 of his previous caps at hooker but moves to the back row with Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Sean Jansen and James McNabney all ruled out. Ireland hope Sheehan's inclusion in the back row will facilitate his powerful ball-carrying capabilities, but he insists he is not going to "overthink" it. "I just get on with stuff. Like, eight on my back, just pick the ball up and go," he said."It can't be that complicated. That's my approach to it, to be honest."Image source, InphoImage caption, Erasmus will watch Saturday's game from South Africa's team hotel Had it not been for the furore surrounding Erasmus, chances are the pre-match talk would have been dominated by scrums. Last year, Ireland were shown five cards and conceded six penalties and a penalty try during a chastening night against the Springbok scrum.  That set-piece shellacking may have given the Irish pack nightmares over the past 12 months, and while South Africa won nine scrum penalties against France, Kolisi expects a closer contest in Dublin this time. "Their scrum is much better than it was a year ago," he said. "You can see they're getting penalties. But our focus is not on what they're going to do. It's about making sure we stick to our plans and do what we need to do in the scrum."The Springboks have been boosted by the return of record cap holder Eben Etzebeth, but his second-row partner Ruan Nortje was ruled out through injury on Friday. He has been replaced by Franco Mostert, who was not originally in the matchday squad.Ireland have also been forced into a late change with Thomas Clarkson replacing Sam Illo as the replacement tight-head prop. The myriad permutations mean Ireland and South Africa could meet again in the finals weekend at Twickenham. Either way, Saturday's sold-out contest in Dublin promises to deliver enough drama to tide fans over until next year's World Cup in Australia, where they could contest the final. Line-ups & officialsIreland: Keenan; Baloucoune, Henshaw, McCloskey, Hansen; Prendergast, Gibson-Park; Porter, Kelleher, Furlong, McCarthy, Beirne, Baird, Van der Flier, Sheehan (capt).Replacements: Stewart, O'Toole, Clarkson, Ryan, Timoney, Casey, Frawley, Aki.South Africa: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Van den Berg; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Mostert, Kolisi (capt), PS du Toit, Hanekom.Replacements: Wessels, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, De Villiers, Van Staden, Williams, Moodie.Referee: C Ridley (RFU)Assistant referees: A Gardner (RA) & A Woodthorpe (RFU)Television match official: Ian Tempest (RFU)Foul play review officer: Tual Trainini (FFR)

title: Pontins fined £1m after grandmother's death at Brean Sands resort
description: Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Wendy Jones, pictured with two of her grandchildren, died after a visit to Pontins Brean Sands in SomersetB
body: Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Wendy Jones, pictured with two of her grandchildren, died after a visit to Pontins Brean Sands in SomersetByRoss PollardClara BullockSomerset and Rebecca WearnBBC investigationsUpdated 3 hours agoPontins holiday park resort has been fined £1m after a grandmother died in a "catastrophic incident" that was "an accident waiting to happen", a judge ruled.Wendy Jones, 68, of Hereford, died six months after a 40m (131ft) section of air conditioning duct and ceiling collapsed onto guests at Pontins' Brean Sands resort, Somerset, in February 2019.On Friday, Pontins' parent firm, Britannia Jinky Jersey, was sentenced at Bristol Crown Court to pay a £1m fine.Jones' son James Havard-Jones said: "There is a temptation to describe what happened as an accident. I cannot do that. An accident is something unforeseeable. This was not unforeseeable. This was preventable."Figure caption, CCTV shows moment ceiling at Pontins collapsesContractor Stephen Bennison also received a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months.They both admitted failure to discharge a duty under health and safety laws.During sentencing, Judge Neil Moody said Bennison was contracted to work on the ceiling because he was cheaper than other bids.Bennison then subcontracted to untrained individuals and failed to carry out a risk assessment, which Judge Moody described as a serious failing."It was an accident waiting to happen. Cutting costs at expense of safety was a factor," he said.Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Bennison received a suspended prison sentenceThe court heard on Thursday that Bennison carried out work on the ceiling despite not being a qualified structural engineer.He ordered more slabs than were needed and it was agreed Bennison would put the leftover slabs on top of the ventilation ducting, the court was told.The prosecution added that "the whole job was done without proper planning on either side". They said it showed the parent company "put profits over safety".Image source, Family HandoutImage caption, Hayley Kendall, Jones' daughter, said life was not the same without her mumJones was one of the 18 people injured during the incident which unfolded ahead of a bingo game.Havard-Jones said in a statement after the trial that the fine is "substantial and should serve as a lesson to other companies that they have to behave properly"."My Mum's life was cut short because of the incompetence and negligence of others."It's been seven long years of anxiety, stress and worry."Jones' daughter Hayley Kendall added: "Nothing will ever replace the loss of our mum. "No-one should ever have to go through what we went through as a family."Det Supt Roger Doxsey, senior investigating officer at Avon and Somerset Police, said the "catastrophic incident lasted a mere matter of seconds", but its consequences are still "painfully felt" seven years on."Wendy's family are absolutely right when they say this incident was entirely preventable."It is a minor miracle, given the weight of the ducting, the nature of its collapse, and the volume of other people present in the Fun Factory at the time of the incident, that more people were not seriously injured and killed," Doxsey added.Image source, Devon and Somerset Fire and RescueImage caption, About 100 people were in the entertainment hall about to play bingo when part of the ceiling and the ducting collapsedThe ruling follows an investigation from BBC News, which exposed how a former site manager at Brean Sands raised concerns at the time that the insulation had been unsafely installed and told Pontins' head office he feared the ceiling would collapse.Brean Sands and Pakefield in Suffolk are currently under contract to house construction workers building Hinkley Point C and Sizewell nuclear plants.Britannia, which bought Pontins out of receivership in 2011, also runs more than 60 hotels across England, Wales and Scotland.Get in touchYour Voice

title: Percy Jackson returns as teenage stars adapt to the limelight
description: Percy Jackson is no ordinary teenager - and neither is the actor tasked with bringing the character to life. As the son of Greek god Poseidon, Percy h
body: Percy Jackson is no ordinary teenager - and neither is the actor tasked with bringing the character to life. As the son of Greek god Poseidon, Percy has demigod status in the hit Disney series and while Walker Scobell doesn't have his powers, that hasn't made the actor's career any less special. The TV series, based on the novels by Rick Riordan, sets figures from Greek mythology and their children in the modern day and returns on Friday for its third instalment - The Titan's Curse.Scobell was 14 when he made his debut as Percy in 2023. Now 17, the US actor says growing up in the spotlight has been an adventure in itself."There's an upside for each downside," he tells BBC Newsbeat."It's a lot easier to get a table at restaurants now and you get to make people's days who are huge Percy Jackson fans just by talking to them for a few minutes. And I think that's a special part of it."But it's not the only part. Earlier this year, Scobell posted on Instagram that he would not be attending his school prom because of death threats sent to girls who live near him.His co-star Aryan Simhadri, who plays Percy's best friend Grover Underwood, has also mentioned uncomfortable meetings with fans.In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, external, he spoke about how "about 40 drunk college girls" recognised him and one tried to put her hand in his back pocket. Since then, he says "fame hasn't been too bad, I've been able to have a normal life because of my parents". "They really make sure when I'm not filming, I'm grounded and I'm planning for my future instead of being enamoured with the aspects of fame."The new series is the first time The Titan's Curse has been adapted on screen.An earlier film adaptation starring Logan Lerman only reached The Sea of Monsters, the second novel in the five-part series.So the cast say they're in uncharted territory for the project - which sees Percy and Grover trying to rescue Annabeth from Kronos's forces."We can make the season in our own weird way because there's nothing you can compare it to, only the book," says Scobell. "So it's the first time we're seeing any of this stuff."Fans have been speculating online what to expect, especially after a shock diversion from the novel at the end of the last series. "I think both book readers and non-book readers are going to be excited and appreciate the tone shift," Simhadri says. "It changes how serious the world is, it's really the start of a new show, not to be dramatic."It's caused a split in opinion from the fanbase, with one fan noting "they are going to stick to the books", but another saying "this is a twist they can get down with".The first series was hugely successful with the opening episode of it reaching 13.3 million viewers, according to entertainment data company Luminate.That dipped to just over 11 million for the second series and the cast is hoping a fresh take on the story will keep fans interested."I personally really like seeing people theorise about what's going to make it," says Simhadri."People who have read the books like talking about how they think we're going to adapt it, I love reading those."It's been a big year for Greek mythology adaptations, with Christopher Nolan's blockbuster The Odyssey getting huge box office numbers and critical acclaim. Leah Sava Jeffries, who plays Athena's daughter Annabeth Chase, says its popularity could be down to how people connect the ancient stories to their own lives."There's stories for everyone," she says."You can have a family where the dad is obsessed with The Odyssey but the children are too young, so they can just watch Percy Jackson. "I feel like there's probably a cooking show about Greek mythology at that point, I mean like there's so many connections no matter what you like."Percy Jackson is released on Disney+ and Hulu on Friday 20 November.

schema.headline: Percy Jackson returns as teenage stars adapt to the limelight

title: South Africa crime statistics: Nearly 600 women killed within three months
description: Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.This figure incl
body: Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week. The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders. Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night.The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, "forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside", police said.The owner's wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made.On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year.General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her.The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park.Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September.The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba's was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region.He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo's death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg.Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area.In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" to find those behind the killings. Last year, he declared that violence against women was a "national disaster".

schema.headline: South Africa crime statistics: Nearly 600 women killed within three months

title: Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case
description: The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change in the way case
body: The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change in the way cases are defended in court.Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period, using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials.Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abusePhilip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers without her knowledge.During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".There is no defined law which states third-party consent is a valid defence.In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone... and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law."This is simply unacceptable."Her calls echo those made by her mother, who spoke on the steps of Winchester Crown Court after the trial."No-one should be able to give it [consent] on your behalf," said Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity."I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in future."Kate Parker, criminal barrister and founder of the Schools Consent Project, said legally, a third party or a partner cannot consent on a person's behalf. "The law makes that very clear. A person consents if he or she agrees by choice and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice," she added."In a case like this where someone has been made unconscious, there is no possible way that that person is able to consent because of course they have no capacity."She added that the defendants' claims that they thought Joanne Young had consented through her husband "doesn't make sense legally, and that's not a legal position that can be supported in court".Parker said the defence used by the four men in the trial is not a correct application of the law but might be something defence lawyers would try and rely on as their client's genuine belief in their victim's consent, or in mitigation to try and get a lower sentence.Like Joanne Young, Laura Bishop from Bristol has also waived her right to anonymity after her ex-husband received a 14-year prison sentence for drugging and raping her while inviting other men to abuse her.Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, Bishop said the crimes will affect her for the rest of her life. "It's something that unfortunately you can never get over," she said."You have to try and remain positive and optimistic but the betrayal, particularly by men, is very difficult to move on from."Bishop has a PhD in cyber crime and uses her expertise and experience to work with MPs and charities to improve governance around digital safety and regulations."The sites my husband used to advertise me are still active and are known by the police to not provide evidence and forensics when asked. "So why are they still accessible?" she said.Bishop understands why many choose to maintain their anonymity but wants to encourage those who can speak out to do so."There's a million reasons why its not be appropriate to waive your anonymity and it might just be because it's something you can't actively do," she said."But for those of us that are able to, we have to stand strong for victims."Debbie Beadle, chief executive officer at Wiltshire-based domestic abuse charity Fear Free, also hopes that Joanne Young's decision to speak out will encourage others to do so."Six in seven rapes against women are done by someone they know and this adds a barrier to people coming forward," she said."The fact that Joanne has come forward will help others when this has happened to them."Zoe Watts is the founder of a global campaign called End Eye Check that works to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse.Like Joanne Young and Bishop, Watts waived her right to anonymity after she was drugged and raped by her husband.Watts hopes that Joanne Young's case "sets a precedent", but told Woman's Hour that the crime is more widespread than many realise."I have had women contact me from 25 different countries," she said. "It's a daily process of women either contacting me because they've woken up to find their husband having sex with them while they're asleep and have done on numerous occasions."Or perhaps they're not sure if they've been drugged or maybe they are genuinely asleep and wake up and find him that way, or women that have found videos or recordings on their phone of things they haven't consented to," Watts added.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, support and information is available at BBC Action Line.Professor Miranda Horvath, director of the University of Suffolk's Institute for Social Justice and Crime, told the BBC that more needs to be done to tackle and "de-platform" perpetrators."The research being conducted and the evidence base we have is emerging [because] these kinds of offences are under-reported and under-detected," she said."We need to ensure proper implementation of the legislation we have through suspect-focused investigation, prosecutions and resourcing and training of the professionals working in these environments."[We also need to be] holding the platforms and tech firms to account that are continuing to proliferate this material and saying 'this is enough, we will not tolerate this in our society'."Prosecutors said Thursday's trial was the first of its kind in England, but former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Jess Phillips, told Radio 4's Woman's Hour that current laws do not do enough to protect women."The law says that somebody can seek a defence to defend themselves against a rape claim if they reasonably believe that they had consent," said Phillips."These people went on to argue that they reasonably believed that Joanne's husband had sought her consent and got it. "They were found guilty, but it's whether the law needs to explicitly say, 'you cannot reasonably believe someone's given consent unless they have given it'."If there was clarity in the law, Joanne wouldn't have been put through the court case," Phillips added.She also believes that more needs to be done to hold the websites hosting adverts and similar content to account."Can every pornographic site in our country categorically say that not one of these snuff videos or sedated videos is on their site? "Unless they can guarantee it with a signed piece of paper from the person that they know is in that video [they should not be published]," Phillips said.
